newsitem.title: USA: U.S. talk radio entering new "mature" period.
newsitem.headline: U.S. talk radio entering new "mature" period.

text.p: Long a cheering section for the right wing of the Republican Party, talk radio is entering a new, more mature, more politically balanced phase, according to radio hosts from around the United States.

Some 15 talk radio hosts who took part in a Washington conference organised by the conservative Heritage Foundation agreed their medium had become a permanent part of the American political landscape. "We have been on a steady climb. We're not a passing phase," said Jim Bohannon of Mutual Broadcasting. "We're here to stay."

Just a couple of years ago talk radio was seen as a dangerous thorn in the side of President Bill Clinton and Democrats in general. Right-wing hosts such as the hugely influential Rush Limbaugh lambasted liberals on a daily basis, helping to whip up the conservative wave that buried Democrats in the 1994 elections and allowed Republicans to take control of both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years.

Two years ago, right-wing columnist Pat Buchanan, who was about to launch an unsuccessful presidential bid, hailed talk radio as a particularly favourable medium for conservatives to communicate with and energise one another. "Many of the right have been radicalized. Now, with talk radio a phone call away, the Silent Majority is silent no longer," he said then.

But things have changed. Talk radio had little discernible effect on the 1996 presidential election and even Limbaugh's influence may have passed its peak as his ratings begin to slip in some markets.
"The 800-pound gorilla is still the 800-pound gorilla but he's losing weight," said Doug Stephan, a talk show host on KABC in Los Angeles.

Two things appear to have happened in the last couple of years. First, Democrats and moderates have started to learn how to use the medium better and there are more liberal talk show hosts and more moderate callers to all shows.
"Talk radio has become more mainstream. Even Democrats have discovered us and want to get on the air, which is a very healthy development," said Dom Giordano, who hosts a programme in Philadelphia.

Second, the audience as a whole seems less interested in politics and less angry at politicians than it was a couple of years ago. Some political hosts have been bounced from prime time in favour of call-in shows about health, sexuality and personal problems. Others have been forced to tackle different issues to hold on to their audiences.
"Crime, celebrity and race -- we are obsessed with all of those three issues," said Victoria Jones of United Stations in New York.
Stephan, from Los Angeles, has seen his focus narrow even further. "We've had 900 days of O.J. on top of O.J. on top of O.J.," he said, referring to the trials of O.J. Simpson.
Mike Siegal, a host in Washington state, said he was dealing more with local issues, which listeners could relate to, rather than launching diatribes on national politics.
In that sense, talk radio may be evolving into a vibrant democratic outlet -- a political Main Street where citizens can air their views on an unlimited range of subjects.
Said Bohannon: "There are a lot of people out there who are tired of ideological extremes. There's nothing wimpy about doing away with left and right extremes."

But Brian Wilson, a Baltimore-based host who broadcasts on many different stations from an avowedly right-wing, libertarian perspective, defended the old pattern of ideological hosts provoking the audience with their firebrand ideas. "Common ground is -- trust me -- boring," he said.
